items.title: Overview
items.text:
Participants will be tested on the content below:

I. For each object in the lists below, identify and explain: surface/atmospheric features; processes (e.g., cryovolcanism), and properties of specific objects:

  1. Objects in the Solar System:

    • Venus
    • Mars
    • Ganymede
    • Europa
    • Enceladus
    • Titan
    • Makemake
    • 101955 Bennu
    • 67P/Churyumov—Gerasimenko

  2. Extrasolar Systems:

    • TRAPPIST-1
    • Kepler-452
    • LHS 1140

II. Habitability beyond the Earth:

  1. Conditions relevant to habitability, including:

    • temperature
    • atmospheric composition and retention
    • presence of stable liquids (surface and subsurface)
    • tidal heating
    • chemical disequilibrium

  2. Geologic and chemical evidence of habitability, including:

    • historical evidence of liquid water from morphology
    • surface/atmospheric composition inferred spectral features
    • delivery of water and organic material from small Solar System bodies

  3. Biology and chemistry relevant to habitability, including:

    • building blocks of life (proteins/nucleic acids/lipids/carbohydrates)
    • phases/forms of water (liquid/amorphous and crystalline ice brines/clathrates)
    • extremophiles (chemolithoautotrophs,tardigrades)

III. General engineering principles and facilities including: science objectives/instrumentation/tradeoffs underlying spacecraft and telescope design

  1. Exoplanet detection techniques, limited to

    • transits
    • radial velocity
    • microlensing,
    • direct imaging.

  2. Space Missions to solar system objects

    • DAVINCI
    • VERITAS
    • Perseverance
    • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
    • MAVEN
    • ESCAPADE
    • Galileo
    • Europa Clipper
    • JUICE
    • Cassini-Huygens
    • Dragonfly
    • OSIRIS-REx
    • Rosetta

  3. Space Telescopes for observng extra-solar-system objects:

    • Kepler Space Telescope
    • James Webb Space Telescope
    • Roman Space Telescope
    • Habitable Worlds Observatory

IV. Mathematical concepts emphasizing algebraic manipulation, including rearranging/deriving equations/order of magnitude estimation/dimensional analysis/sketching graphs/proportions

  1. Light radiation, and temperature

    • Doppler shift
    • flux
    • inverse-square law
    • albedo
    • the Stefan—Boltzmann law
    • Wien’s displacement law
    • equilibrium temperature _

  2. Gravity orbits, and tides:

    • kinetic and potential energy
    • Newton’s law of gravitation
    • Kepler’s laws
    • escape velocity
    • tidal forces

  3. Chemistry:

    • ideal gas law
    • kinetics (e.g. Arrhenius equation) *chemical equilibrium

items.title: Requirements for bacterial life
items.text:
• A Stable Star

Very young stars and very old stars, and have highly variable luminosity, and significant, sporadic mass loss. Middle-aged stars like the sun are more stable, both in luminosity and in mass ejection.

  • A nearly circular orbit

Planets whose radius from the central star remains stable will not undergo large variations in temperature, especially variations large enough to cause freezing or boiling. Some life may tolerate long freezing periods, but none will tolerate boiling.

This requirement also rules out double stars and multiple star systems.

items.title: Requirements for aerobic life
items.text:
Aeroboic life requires a stable atmosphere to breath. The retention of an atmosphere imposes further restrictions on habitable exoplanets:

  • a secondary atmosphere. The first atmosphere of a planet would be hydrogen, its most abundant gas. But this gas is quickly swept away by any solar wind. Thus, habitable planets require some "engine" to create and then maintan that atmosphere. Earth's atmosphere is continually regenerated by volcanic and tectonic activity.

  • surface water, which implies the average surface temperature must fall in the range 0 to 100C.

  • a stable energy budget. That is, a balance between [the heat gained from the central star and internal sources] and [the heat lost by thermal emission and not trapped by the planet's atmosphere].

  • effective mechanisms to transport energy around the exoplanet. This includes winds and air currents to move heat from hot zones to cold zones, ocean currents to moderate extreme weather, and a planetary tilt that prevents wild seasonal variations.

  • a global-scale magnetic field to repel energetic particles in the solar wind

items.title: A stable star
items.text: A central star with limited time variability is necessary to maintain a planetary temperature in the narrow range required for life.

items.title: A nearly circular orbit in the habitable zone
items.text: A highly elliptical orbit could cause its inhabitants to freeze or boil, which might. Freezing might not kill existing life, but boiling would of course.

items.title: A stable and nearly ubiquitous supply of water
items.text: Life, including its necessary food supply, can only exist in the vicinity of a body of water.

items.title: A "secondary" atmosphere
items.text:
Presumably, the primary atmosphere is mostly hydrogen, and is rapidly blown off by the stellar wind.

A secondary atmosphere can protect the planet from ultraviolet solar radiation.

However, if that secondary atmosphere is too "thick" (due to too much volcanic activity) then it can trap solar radiation, and therefore raise the temperature of both the atmosphere and the planet. This is what's happened to Venus, whose daytime temperature is 310K, far above the boiling point of water.

items.title: A magnetic field
items.text:
The magnetic field must be sufficient to repel the stellar wind and cosmic rays which would otherwise blow away its atmosphere.

Presumably, this magnetic field would be created by a partially liquid, active core. That activity (e.g. volcanism and/or plate tectonics) must be sufficient to maintain the planet's secondary atmosphere against the dissipative effects of the steallar wind.

The Mars carbonate catastrophe, is thought to have caused the interior to solidify and therefore fail to maintain its secondary atmosphere.

Venus has two problems:

  • unlike Earth, Venus' surface is not made of moving crustal plates, allowing heat to build up in its core.

  • Venus' core doesn't undergo convection because Venus rotates so slowly (243 Earth days). Therefore Coriolis forces are unable to make a magnetic dynamo.

items.title: Why focus on low-mass stars?
items.text:
Compared to massive stars:

  • Low-mass stars are more common. So the neighborhood of the Sun is more likely to be crowded with low-mass stars than high-mass stars.

  • Low-mass stars are smaller. So when a planet-sized objects eclipses a low-mass star, it hides a larger fraction of its surface.

  • Low-mass stars have lower mass, so planet-sized objects will cause a relatively larger perturbation in the star's radial velocity.

items.title: Kepler 452b
items.text:
Kepler 452 is much more hotter, and therefore more luminous, than the other stars that are part of this Science Olympiad. Luminous stars are rarer than the cool dwarf stars, and can therefore be detected at much larger distances. Kepler 452 is about 10x more distant than the cool M stars mentioned earlier.

Kepler 452b, the first exoplanet associated with Kepler 452, has many parameters similar to Earth: Th object is thought to be "the most Earth-like" planet yet discovered. See below:

Earth Kepler 452b Temperature of central star 5778K 5757K Size of associated star Period of orbit 365d 385d Size of planet 1 R\(_{\text Earth}\) 1.6 R\(_{\text Earth}\) Estimated Temperature 255K 265K

The discovery of Kepler 452b, announced by NASA on July 23, 2015 exploited two key advantages of the Kepler Space Telescope:.

  • the Kepler Space Telescope is immune to the image blurring caused by the Earth's atmsosphere,

  • the Kepler Space Telescope is about \(sim5\times\) larger than the telescopes used for the TRAPPIST or MEarth projects, and therefore has higher intrinsic spatial resolution.

(Ground-based telescopes still have one significant advantage, i.e., they are still operational, whereas Kepler Space Telescope exhausted its supply of fuel by 2018.)

During its operational lifetime, Kepler searched a single patch of sky (115 square degrees, roughly 12-16 degrees in diameter) in the constellations Cygnus and Lyra, and monitored approximately 150,000 stars in that region.

The Kepler telescope repeatedly measured the position of each star in their program; those with the highest proper motions were the nearest, and therefore best candidates for finding planetary companions. Kepler monitoried these nearby stars in search of small but repeatable dips in their brightness, indicative of a planet passing in front of the star. By this means Kepler discovered 2,784 exoplanets; 2,000 additional planetary candidates await confirmation.

Kepler 452b is the first near-Earth-size planet found orbiting in the habitable zone of a sun-like (G-type) star rather than a dim red dwarf. This match in both star type and orbital conditions makes it a key milestone in the search for an Earth twin.

items.title: LHS 1140b
items.text:
LHS 1140 b was discovered by the MEarth project which is similar to the TRAPPIST project in that it uses robotically-run telescopes which are located in both hemispheres:

  • the Northern Hemisphere site is at Mt. Hopkins, AZ (just west of Tucson), and
  • the Southern Hemisphere site is at Cerro Tololo.

Unlike the TRAPPIST project, each site contains 8 telescopes, though each of the telescopes is smaller (16", 0.4m diamter) than the telescopes used in the TRAPPIST project.

items.title: Selecting target stars by proper motion
items.text: The LHS (Luyten Half-Second) Catalogue is a compilation of about 4000 stars that are moving fast relative to our solar system, and are therefore thought to be nearby. It was originally (1979) compiled from the photographic plates of the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, combined with second-epoch plates (taken about 5 years after the first) of selected areas. A second Palomar Sky Survey was carried out in the 1990's, and its plates were contemporaneously digitized. The digitized version of the Second Survey, distributed in 2006, was the basis for the Revised LHS catalog.

items.title: Trappist 1b,c,d,e,f,g,h
items.text:
TRAPPIST-1 is the name given to the first (and only) star with evidence of exoplanets found by the TRAPPIST facilities, a pair of matching 0.6m telescopes located

  • one in the Southern Hemisphere at La Silla in Chile;

  • one in the Northern Hemisphere at the Oukaimeden Observatory in Morocco.

The TRAPPIST telescopes and their operation are a Belgian project, named after the monks who brewed Belgian beers. The name is also an acronym for TRansiting Planets and Planetisimals and plAnetiesimals Small Portable Service Telescope.

Both TRAPPIST telescopes are robotic, i.e., run under computer control by a remote observer(s), possibly in Europe.

The TRAPPIST project focusses on ultra-cool dwarf stars drawn from public star catalogues, e.g., 2MASS.

The pilot catalog consisted of about 50-60 of the brightest southern ultra-cool dwarfs; only the star designated TRAPPIST-1 was found to have exoplanets.

The image below shows the field of view (1.6 arcmin \(\times\) 1.6 arcmin) as seen in visible light near TRAPPIST-1:

The innermost planets (b,c,d) lack thick atmospheres.

The following 4 planets are theoretically in the habitable zone.

  • TRAPPIST-1e: Widely considered the best candidate for life, with a size and energy input most similar to a rocky Earth-like world.

  • TRAPPIST-1f: Located a bit further out in a cooler region, potentially requiring thick greenhouse gases to maintain surface water.

  • TRAPPIST-1g: Sits near the outer edge of the zone, running the risk of being a cold, ice-covered world.

  • TRAPPIST-1d: Positioned on the inner edge; newer data suggests it might be too warm or lack a substantial atmosphere.

Note that, because these planets orbit close to the central star, they are all likely to be tidally locked, meaning the same side always faces the star.

items.title: 101955 Bennu, an asteroid
items.text: Astronomers have found that asteroids in different "classes" (based on color) have different sized and differently shaped orbits. This suggests that asteroids in different classes originated by different processes.

items.title: Bennus's Asteroid Type based on color
items.text:
In the 1970's classification of Asteroids, Bennu is classified as a "C" type asteroid because it is dark, implying its surface is covered in primitive, carbon-rich material.. Comets in this broad category are packed with carbon compounds, primitive organics, and volatile elements dating back over 4.5 billion years to the formation of the solar system.

Spectroscopic data from missions like OSIRIS-REx have allowed more precise classifications based on both color and spectral features. In the newer (2002) Bus and Binzel classification scheme, (which is called a "taxonomy" rather than a spectral class) Bennu is classified as a B-class asteroid.

items.title: Bennus's Asteroid Type based on orbit
items.text:
From its orbit, 101955 is classified as an "Apollo class" asteroid, because it has a semi-major axis \(>1\) AU and a semi-minor axis \(<1\) AU, and it therefore crosses the Earth's orbit.

Apollo class asteroids make up the largest group of near-Earth objects.
